description_full: Organo Corporation operates as a water treatment engineering company in Japan, Taiwan, the United States, China, Southeast Asia, and internationally. The company engages in the manufacturing, sales, and maintenance of various water and wastewater treatment systems utilizing ion exchange resins, separation membranes, activated carbon, etc.; provision of water treatment outsourcing services; and sales of various water treatment chemicals and food processing materials. Its products include filtration equipment: soft water systems; pure and ultrapure water systems; tabletop pure and ultrapure water systems; filters; water treatment facilities; water treatment chemicals; ion-exchange resin and replenishment material; and other technologies and services. The company also provides remote monitoring; maintenance planning, scheduled inspections, and supplying of consumables; equipment diagnostics, equipment enhancement, and modification work; and equipment-owned service model services. It provides its products and services to electronics; pharmaceutical and cosmetics; chemicals and machinery; food and beverages; thermal and nuclear power plant; water and sewage treatment plants; healthcare and research institutions; convenience stores and restaurants; and buildings and commercial facilities. The company was formerly known as Japan Organo Co., Ltd. and changed its name to Organo Corporation in 1966. Organo Corporation was incorporated in 1941 and is headquartered in Koto, Japan.

financial_summary: Organo Corp. is a mid-cap industrials business with a $3.8B market cap on $1.1B of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at +6% over the past three years, a respectable pace for a business of this size. Operating margins are expanding by +3.2pp year-over-year, which is one of the strongest signals that the moat is deepening.
Returns on capital run at 20% against a 9% cost of capital — a 11-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat, with gross margins sitting at 31%.

The business throws off $64M in free cash flow — roughly 6 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders. Cash conversion is thin at 0.46×, however, which raises the oldest question in analysis: are these earnings backed by cash?.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year.

Shareholder yield is only 1.4%, a thin return of capital, and insiders hold 44% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and within its sector the business captures 1.9× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.
